definition: A unique numerical identifier assigned to every device connected to the internet, functioning like a digital postal address that allows devices to find and communicate with each other.
metaDescription: Learn what an IP address is, why it matters for privacy, and how this unique identifier can reveal your location and online activities.
simpleExplanation: Think of an IP address like your home's mailing address, but for your computer or phone on the internet. Every time you go online, your device gets assigned a number that websites can see and use to send information back to you.
whyItMatters: Your IP address can reveal your approximate location, internet provider, and can be used to track your online activities across websites. This makes it a key piece of personal information that affects your digital privacy.
technicalDetail: IP addresses come in two formats: IPv4 (like 192.168.1.1) with about 4.3 billion possible addresses, and IPv6 (like 2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:0370:7334) with vastly more combinations. They can be static (permanent) or dynamic (changing), and may be shared among multiple devices through NAT.

examples.explanation: When you visit Amazon.com, the website can see your IP address (like 203.0.113.45) and might use it to show prices in your local currency or comply with regional laws.
Netflix checks your IP address to determine your country and only shows content licensed for that region, which is why available shows differ by location.
Ad networks collect IP addresses to build profiles and target ads based on your general location, even across different websites you visit.
